passages.title: The Vanishing Reading Room
passages.text: Every few months a district headquarters inaugurates a gleaming digital library, complete with tablets, charging docks and a ribbon-cutting ceremony. Meanwhile, three kilometres away, the old panchayat reading room, its shelves sagging and its single ceiling fan idle, is quietly shut for want of a caretaker whose honorarium was never sanctioned. The contrast is instructive. Officials are fond of counting devices because devices can be counted; they are far less comfortable with the harder arithmetic of habit. A reading culture is not purchased in a single budget cycle. It grows around a patient librarian who knows which child is ready for which book, around a corner where a farmer may borrow an almanac without being questioned, around the unglamorous guarantee that the door will be open on Tuesday as it was on Monday. Technology can certainly widen that circle, but it cannot replace the human anchor at its centre. Before we celebrate another launch, we might ask a plainer question: how many of last year's new libraries still have a living, funded, reasonably cheerful person behind the desk?

passages.title: The Weaver at Dusk
passages.text:
He does not hurry the shuttle now;
the light has thinned to a single thread,
and the loom, that old accountant of days,
tallies each passing in warp and weft.
His father's knots are in this cloth,
his daughter's colour in its border,
and somewhere in the middle, unplanned,
a grey he cannot trace to any cause.
Buyers will call the flaw a charm
and pay a little less for charm.
He smiles, for a man who has worn
his whole life as an apprenticeship
knows that the pattern is never finished,
only put down, like a tired hand,
until the morning asks for it again.

passages.title: Sleep and the Making of Memory
passages.text: For decades, sleep was regarded as a passive interval in which the brain, like a machine switched off at the mains, merely rested. Recording studies have overturned this view. During slow-wave sleep, patterns of neural firing that occurred while an animal learned a maze are replayed, often at greater speed, as though the brain were rehearsing the day's lessons. This replay is thought to help transfer fragile, newly formed traces from the hippocampus, which stores them temporarily, to the neocortex, where they are integrated with existing knowledge. Crucially, the process appears selective: memories tagged as emotionally salient or relevant to future goals are strengthened, while trivial details fade. Researchers are cautious, however. Disrupting sleep impairs learning, but this correlation does not prove that replay itself is the causal mechanism, since sleep deprivation also alters mood, attention and hormone levels. Some experiments that played faint cues linked to a learned task during sleep have yielded improved recall, yet the effects are modest. Thus, while the picture is compelling, it remains incomplete, and claims that one can master a language by listening to recordings overnight go far beyond the evidence.

questions.question: Hardly had the chairman begun his speech ____ the lights went out.
questions.explanation: "Hardly/Scarcely ... when" is the fixed correlative pair; "than" goes with "No sooner". "Then" and "while" do not form this pattern.

questions.question: At this time tomorrow, the Minister ____ over the Bastar region.
questions.explanation: A fixed point in the future ("at this time tomorrow") needs the future continuous. "Will have flown" shows completion before that time; "would be flying" is a past-in-future form.

questions.question: If I had taken the morning train, I ____ in the examination hall now.
questions.explanation: A past unreal condition with a present result is a mixed conditional: if + past perfect, would + base verb. "Would have been sitting" refers to a past result, not "now".

questions.question: Had it not been for your timely help, I ____ the examination.
questions.explanation: "Had it not been for" is an inverted third conditional (if it had not been for), so the main clause takes "would have + past participle".

questions.question: Ranjan is the only one of the students who ____ passed the Olympiad.
questions.explanation: In "the only one ... who", the relative pronoun refers to the singular "one", so the verb is singular: "has". (With "one of the students who", it would be plural.)

questions.question: Nobody called while I was out, ____?
questions.explanation: Nobody has a negative meaning, so the tag is positive; the pronoun "they" is used for indefinite pronouns like nobody/somebody. The tag follows the main verb "called" (did).

questions.question: He said, "I will have finished the report by the time you arrive tomorrow." Choose the correct indirect speech.
options: He said that he will have finished the report by the time you arrive tomorrow.
He said that he would finish the report by the time I arrive the next day.
He said that he had finished the report by the time I would arrive the next day.
He said that he would have finished the report by the time I arrived the next day.
questions.explanation: The reporting verb is past, so "will have finished" becomes "would have finished", "arrive" becomes "arrived", "you" becomes "I", and "tomorrow" becomes "the next day".

questions.question: The speaker has only one brother. Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: My brother who lives in Durg is an engineer.
My brother, who lives in Durg is an engineer.
My brother, who lives in Durg, is an engineer.
My brother who, lives in Durg, is an engineer.
questions.explanation: Since there is only one brother, the clause adds extra (non-defining) information and must be set off by a pair of commas. A defining clause (no commas) would imply several brothers.

questions.question: Which sentence has NO dangling modifier?
options: Walking through the forest, the tall sal trees impressed us.
Walking through the forest, we were impressed by the tall sal trees.
Having finished the exam, the bell rang.
Driving down the road, the mountains came into view.
questions.explanation: The participle phrase must modify the subject of the main clause. Only in the correct option is the doer of "walking" ("we") the subject; in the others trees, bell and mountains cannot walk, finish or drive.

questions.question: She wanted me to attend the seminar, but I didn't want ____.
questions.explanation: Ellipsis of the repeated infinitive phrase leaves "to" (the "reduced infinitive"): "I didn't want to (attend)". "So" is used after think/say/hope, not after want.

questions.question: The ground is wet, but I slept early and cannot be sure. It ____ last night.
questions.explanation: "May have + V3" expresses possibility in the past; "must have" shows strong certainty, which the speaker lacks. "Should have" shows criticism/expectation, and "can have" is not used in affirmative speculation.

questions.question: The scholar offered ____ information about the manuscript, so we could barely trace its origin.
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable, and "barely" signals a negative sense, so "little" is correct. "Few", "many" and "several" go only with plural countable nouns.

questions.question: He tried to talk his sister ____ the idea of quitting her job.
questions.explanation: "Talk someone out of" means to dissuade. "Talk into" means to persuade to do something, "talk over" means to discuss, and "talk off" is not a standard phrasal verb.

questions.question: Which is the simple-sentence form of "Because he was ill, he could not attend the meeting"?
options: Owing to his illness, he could not attend the meeting.
He was ill, so he could not attend the meeting.
He could not attend the meeting as he was ill.
Though he was ill, he attended the meeting.
questions.explanation: A simple sentence has one finite verb; the adverb clause becomes a phrase ("Owing to his illness"). Option 2 is compound, option 3 is complex, option 4 changes the meaning.

questions.question: It was only after the results were declared ____ she realised her error.
questions.explanation: An it-cleft has the pattern "It was + focused element + that ...". "When", "which" and "then" cannot introduce the clefted clause here.

questions.question: A "misanthrope" is a person who
questions.explanation: Greek miseo (hate) + anthropos (human being). "Hating women" is "misogynist", while "loving humanity" is "philanthropist".

questions.question: In the phrase "a sound argument", the word "sound" means
questions.explanation: "Sound" as an adjective means reliable/logically valid. The others are different senses (noun: noise; noun: strait; verb: fathom).

questions.question: The mild sauce was a perfect ____ to the spicy curry.
questions.explanation: "Complement" means something that completes or balances. "Compliment" is praise (a homophone), and the others do not fit.

questions.question: The cyclone ____ havoc along the coast.
questions.explanation: "Wreak havoc" is the fixed collocation; "wrecked" and the others are look-alike distractors.

questions.question: In which sentence is an adjective used as a noun?
options: The wounded were taken to the camp hospital.
The wounded soldier was taken to the camp hospital.
questions.explanation: In "The wounded were taken", "the wounded" means "wounded people" and is the subject of the sentence. In the other options "wounded" is an adjective or a verb form.

questions.question: A "lexical bundle" is best described as
options: an idiom whose meaning cannot be guessed from its words
a group of words with the same root
a set of words that sound alike
a recurrent sequence of three or more words that frequently co-occur, whether or not it is idiomatic
questions.explanation: Lexical bundles (e.g. "on the other hand", "as a result of") are identified by frequency, not by opacity or morphology, which distinguishes them from idioms.

questions.question: A "Sisyphean" task is one that is
options: endless and futile, however hard one works
questions.explanation: Sisyphus, in Greek myth, was condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever; it rolled back each time. Hence an endless, unrewarding labour.

questions.question: In "The Crown rejected the petition", the word "Crown" stands for the monarch or government. This figure of speech is
questions.explanation: The name of an associated object (the Crown) replaces the thing meant (the monarchy): metonymy. Synecdoche uses a part for the whole; there is no comparison (simile) or address to an absent person (apostrophe).

questions.question: In "He caught the train and a cold", the figure of speech is
questions.explanation: One verb ("caught") governs two objects in different senses (physical vs. illness): zeugma. Pleonasm is redundancy; hendiadys expresses one idea through two nouns.

questions.question: "All hands on deck!" shouted the captain. The figure of speech used is
questions.explanation: "Hands" (a part) stands for the whole sailors: synecdoche. Metonymy substitutes an associated name, not a part of the thing.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of litotes?
options: It was no small feat to cross the Hasdeo forest on foot.
questions.explanation: Litotes affirms something by negating its opposite ("no small feat" = a great feat). "Deafening silence" is an oxymoron; the others are metaphors.

questions.question: In "of the people, by the people, for the people", the repetition of the same words at the END of successive phrases is called
questions.explanation: Epistrophe repeats words at the end of clauses; anaphora repeats at the beginning; anadiplosis repeats the last word of one clause at the start of the next.

questions.question: Which of the following words was formed by back-formation?
questions.explanation: Back-formation creates a shorter word by removing a (supposed) affix: "editor" gave "edit". The others are formed by adding affixes.

questions.question: The verb "cleave" is a contronym because it
options: is both a noun and a verb
has two opposite meanings: to split and to cling
questions.explanation: A contronym (auto-antonym) carries opposite senses: "cleave" means to split apart and also to adhere closely.

questions.question: To "rest on one's laurels" means to
options: be content with past achievements and make no further effort
questions.explanation: The laurel wreath symbolised victory; resting on it means complacency after earlier success.

questions.question: The description of the old reading room with sagging shelves and an idle fan mainly serves to
options: advertise the reading room to visitors
suggest that fans should be repaired
show how a modest, useful institution is neglected while showpieces are celebrated
questions.explanation: The image sets the neglected, caretaker-less room against the gleaming launch, illustrating the contrast the author calls instructive.

questions.question: The phrase "the harder arithmetic of habit" suggests that
options: building lasting reading habits is difficult and cannot be measured by simply counting devices
questions.explanation: The contrast is between easily countable devices and the slow, hard-to-quantify work of forming habits. The phrase is figurative, not literal.

questions.question: The author's tone in the passage is best described as
questions.explanation: Remarks like "fond of counting devices because devices can be counted" and the "reasonably cheerful person" are gently ironic criticism, not outright hostility or neutral reporting.

questions.question: In the passage, the expression "human anchor" most nearly refers to
options: a patient, funded librarian who keeps the library steady
a heavy piece of library furniture
an official who cuts the ribbon
questions.explanation: The "human anchor at its centre" is the patient librarian who knows each reader and keeps the service dependable.

questions.question: The closing question of the passage mainly serves to
options: ask readers for statistics on new libraries
express doubt about the existence of libraries
shift the test of success from launching libraries to keeping them staffed and functioning
questions.explanation: It is a rhetorical question: it redefines the measure of success as continued staffed service, thus summing up the editorial's argument.

questions.question: The expression "that old accountant of days" is an example of
questions.explanation: The loom is directly identified with an accountant (it "tallies" passing time) without "like" or "as": a metaphor.

questions.question: The lines "Buyers will call the flaw a charm / and pay a little less for charm" bring out
options: the weaver's anger at dishonest buyers
the irony that imperfection is praised but still undervalued
the superior quality of machine-made cloth
the weaver's plan to raise prices
questions.explanation: Buyers verbally admire the flaw yet pay less, which is ironic. The poem does not state anger or machine competition.

questions.question: The overall mood of the poem is one of
questions.explanation: He does not hurry, "smiles", and views the work as continuing. The mood is contemplative and accepting, not bitter or despairing.

questions.question: "The pattern is never finished, only put down, like a tired hand" suggests that
options: the weaver is too tired to work again
the cloth was left incomplete because of an accident
a lifetime of craft is a continuing process, interrupted but not completed
questions.explanation: The simile pictures work as paused rather than ended, resuming "until the morning asks for it again".

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the poem?
options: The craft has been passed through generations.
The weaver works slowly as evening comes.
The weaver bitterly blames the buyers for the flaw.
The cloth contains an unplanned flaw.
questions.explanation: The weaver smiles; no blame is stated. "Father's knots ... daughter's colour" supports generations, and "does not hurry" and "light has thinned" support the other options.

questions.question: The main purpose of the passage is to
options: prove that sleep replay causes all learning
outline the evolving evidence on sleep and memory while cautioning about its limits
argue that sleep is unnecessary for adults
questions.explanation: The passage reviews findings (replay, transfer, selectivity) and then qualifies them ("cautious", "incomplete").

questions.question: The comparison "like a machine switched off at the mains" is used to
options: illustrate the earlier belief that sleep is a passive state
describe how neurons fire in slow-wave sleep
show that the brain needs electricity
questions.explanation: It is a simile used for the old view; the passage immediately says the view has been "overturned".

questions.question: The author would most probably regard the claim that one can master a language by overnight listening as
questions.explanation: The last sentence says such claims "go far beyond the evidence"; the cue experiments only showed modest effects.

questions.question: Which statement CANNOT be inferred from the passage?
options: Memory traces may move from the hippocampus to the neocortex during sleep.
Some memories are strengthened more than others during sleep.
Sleep deprivation affects only memory and nothing else.
The link between replay and learning is not fully proven.
questions.explanation: The passage states sleep deprivation also alters mood, attention and hormones, contradicting option 1; the others are supported.

questions.question: The word "compelling" in "the picture is compelling" most nearly means
questions.explanation: Used of a picture or argument, "compelling" means persuasive/convincing, consistent with the author's balanced approval before saying it is incomplete.

questions.question: According to Krashen's Affective Filter Hypothesis, the filter is raised (acquisition is blocked) mainly by
questions.questionHi: क्रैशेन की Affective Filter परिकल्पना के अनुसार filter (भाषा अर्जन में बाधा) मुख्यतः किससे बढ़ता है?
questions.explanation: Anxiety, low self-esteem and low motivation raise the affective filter so that input is not taken in; motivation, confidence and low anxiety lower it.
questions.explanationHi: चिंता, कम आत्म-सम्मान और कम प्रेरणा filter को बढ़ाते हैं जिससे input ग्रहण नहीं हो पाता; प्रेरणा, आत्मविश्वास और कम चिंता filter को घटाते हैं।

questions.question: A child keeps asking "Why is the sky blue?" Which Halliday function is mainly being used?
questions.questionHi: एक बच्चा बार-बार पूछता है "आसमान नीला क्यों है?" हैलिडे का कौन-सा भाषा-प्रकार्य मुख्यतः प्रयुक्त हो रहा है?
questions.explanation: Halliday's heuristic function is language used to explore and learn about the environment, as in questions seeking explanations.
questions.explanationHi: हैलिडे का heuristic प्रकार्य भाषा द्वारा परिवेश को जानने-समझने के लिए है, जैसे स्पष्टीकरण माँगने वाले प्रश्न।

questions.question: Long's Interaction Hypothesis stresses that language acquisition is best promoted by
questions.questionHi: लॉन्ग की Interaction Hypothesis के अनुसार भाषा अर्जन को सबसे अधिक बढ़ावा किससे मिलता है?
optionsHi: बातचीत के दौरान अर्थ की बातचीत (negotiation of meaning)
questions.explanation: When learners and interlocutors clarify, confirm and repair misunderstandings, input becomes comprehensible and acquisition is aided.
questions.explanationHi: जब बातचीत में सीखने वाले और वक्ता स्पष्टीकरण, पुष्टि और सुधार करते हैं तो input समझने योग्य बनता है और अर्जन में मदद मिलती है।

questions.question: In second-language acquisition, "fossilisation" (Selinker) refers to
questions.questionHi: द्वितीय भाषा अर्जन में "fossilisation" (सेलिंकर) का अर्थ है
options: rapid improvement after a long gap
permanent persistence of non-target forms in the learner's interlanguage despite exposure and instruction
optionsHi: लंबे अंतराल के बाद तेज़ सुधार
अवसर और शिक्षण के बावजूद सीखने वाले की interlanguage में लक्ष्य-भाषा से भिन्न रूपों का स्थायी बने रहना
questions.explanation: Selinker used fossilisation for errors that become stable in interlanguage and resist correction despite continued input and instruction.
questions.explanationHi: सेलिंकर ने fossilisation उन त्रुटियों के लिए कहा जो interlanguage में स्थिर हो जाती हैं और लगातार input व शिक्षण के बावजूद नहीं सुधरतीं।

questions.question: In the revised Bloom taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl), the highest cognitive level is
questions.questionHi: संशोधित ब्लूम टैक्सोनॉमी (एंडरसन व क्रेथवोल) में सर्वोच्च ज्ञानात्मक स्तर कौन-सा है?
questions.explanation: The revision reordered the top levels: Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analysing, Evaluating, Creating. Creating (e.g. writing an original story) is highest.
questions.explanationHi: संशोधन में क्रम है: Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analysing, Evaluating, Creating। Creating (जैसे मौलिक कहानी लिखना) सर्वोच्च है।

questions.question: A child who keeps asking "Why does the moon change shape?" is using which of Halliday's early functions of language?
questions.questionHi: एक बच्चा बार-बार पूछता है "चाँद का आकार क्यों बदलता है?" वह हैलिडे के भाषा के किस प्रकार्य (function) का प्रयोग कर रहा है?
questions.explanation: The heuristic function is language used to explore and learn about the environment (asking questions). Regulatory controls others, instrumental satisfies needs, imaginative creates imaginary worlds.
questions.explanationHi: Heuristic प्रकार्य में भाषा का प्रयोग वातावरण के बारे में जानने के लिए प्रश्न पूछने में होता है। Regulatory दूसरों को नियंत्रित करता है, instrumental आवश्यकता पूरी करता है और imaginative कल्पना की दुनिया रचता है।

questions.question: A learner forgets the word "umbrella" and says "the thing we open in rain to protect from water". In Canale and Swain's model, this shows
questions.questionHi: एक विद्यार्थी "umbrella" शब्द भूल जाता है और कहता है "वह चीज़ जिसे हम बारिश में खोलते हैं"। Canale और Swain के मॉडल में यह क्या दर्शाता है?
questions.explanation: Using circumlocution to overcome a communication gap is a communication strategy, i.e. strategic competence.
questions.explanationHi: संवाद की कमी को घुमा-फिराकर कहकर पूरा करना communication strategy है, यानी strategic competence।

questions.question: In Canale and Swain's framework, "strategic competence" refers to
questions.questionHi: कैनेल और स्वेन के ढाँचे में "strategic competence" का अर्थ है
options: using verbal and non-verbal strategies, such as paraphrase, to compensate for communication breakdowns
optionsHi: संप्रेषण में आई बाधा की भरपाई के लिए paraphrase जैसी मौखिक व अमौखिक युक्तियों का प्रयोग
questions.explanation: Strategic competence is the ability to compensate for gaps in knowledge or breakdowns in communication, e.g. by circumlocution, gestures or asking for repetition.
questions.explanationHi: Strategic competence ज्ञान की कमी या संप्रेषण-बाधा की भरपाई करने की क्षमता है, जैसे घुमाकर कहना, इशारे या दोहराने का अनुरोध।

questions.question: In second-language acquisition, "fossilisation" refers to
questions.questionHi: द्वितीय भाषा अर्जन में "fossilisation" का अर्थ है
options: a learner's complete mastery of the target language
the loss of the mother tongue
persistent non-target forms that remain in a learner's speech despite exposure and instruction
a method of teaching old texts
optionsHi: सीखने वाले की भाषा में लगातार बने रहने वाले गलत रूप, जो अभ्यास और शिक्षण के बाद भी नहीं जाते
पुराने पाठों को पढ़ाने की विधि
questions.explanation: Selinker used the term for errors that become permanently stabilised in interlanguage, resisting correction.
questions.explanationHi: सेलिंकर ने यह शब्द उन त्रुटियों के लिए प्रयोग किया जो interlanguage में स्थायी हो जाती हैं और सुधार का विरोध करती हैं।

questions.question: In the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl), a task asking learners to design an advertisement in English for a school fair belongs to which level?
questions.questionHi: संशोधित ब्लूम टैक्सोनॉमी (एंडरसन और क्रैथवोल) में विद्यार्थियों से स्कूल मेले के लिए अंग्रेज़ी में विज्ञापन डिज़ाइन करने को कहना किस स्तर में आता है?
questions.explanation: Designing and producing something new is the top level, Creating. Remembering is recall, Understanding is explaining, Applying is using known procedures in a given situation.
questions.explanationHi: कुछ नया डिज़ाइन और निर्मित करना सर्वोच्च स्तर Creating है। Remembering याद करना है, Understanding समझाना है और Applying ज्ञात विधियों का प्रयोग है।

questions.question: A teacher gives a sentence frame for a paragraph, then provides less and less help as learners improve. The gradual withdrawal of support is called
questions.questionHi: शिक्षक अनुच्छेद लिखने के लिए वाक्य-ढाँचा देता है और विद्यार्थियों के सुधरने पर सहायता कम करता जाता है। सहायता को धीरे-धीरे हटाना क्या कहलाता है?
questions.explanation: In Vygotskian scaffolding, support is temporary within the ZPD and is faded as the learner becomes independent.
questions.explanationHi: वाइगोत्स्की के scaffolding में सहायता ZPD के भीतर अस्थायी होती है और विद्यार्थी के स्वतंत्र होते ही हटा ली जाती है (fading)।

questions.question: Which set represents Coyle's 4Cs framework for CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning)?
questions.questionHi: CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) के लिए कॉयल के 4Cs ढाँचे का सही समूह कौन-सा है?
questions.explanation: Coyle's 4Cs are Content (subject matter), Cognition (thinking), Communication (language) and Culture (intercultural awareness).
questions.explanationHi: कॉयल के 4Cs हैं: Content (विषयवस्तु), Cognition (चिंतन), Communication (भाषा) और Culture (अंतर-सांस्कृतिक समझ)।

questions.question: A teacher lets learners discuss an English story in Hindi or Chhattisgarhi and then write about it in English. This strategy is best called
questions.questionHi: एक शिक्षक विद्यार्थियों को अंग्रेज़ी कहानी पर हिंदी या छत्तीसगढ़ी में चर्चा करने देता है और फिर अंग्रेज़ी में लिखवाता है। इस युक्ति को सबसे उपयुक्त रूप से क्या कहेंगे?
questions.explanation: Translanguaging uses learners' full linguistic repertoire as a resource for learning; it contrasts with strict English-only immersion.
questions.explanationHi: Translanguaging में विद्यार्थियों की सभी भाषाओं को सीखने के संसाधन के रूप में प्रयोग किया जाता है; यह केवल-अंग्रेज़ी immersion से भिन्न है।

questions.question: A learner reads aloud accurately but cannot answer inferential questions. The most appropriate diagnosis is a weakness in
questions.questionHi: एक विद्यार्थी शुद्ध पढ़ लेता है, पर अनुमानात्मक प्रश्नों के उत्तर नहीं दे पाता। सबसे उपयुक्त निदान किस क्षेत्र की कमज़ोरी है?
optionsHi: बोध और अनुमान लगाने की क्षमता, डिकोडिंग की नहीं
questions.explanation: Accurate reading shows decoding and pronunciation are adequate; the difficulty lies at the level of meaning-making, so remediation should target inference skills.
questions.explanationHi: शुद्ध वाचन दर्शाता है कि डिकोडिंग और उच्चारण ठीक हैं; कठिनाई अर्थ-निर्माण में है, इसलिए उपचार अनुमान-कौशल पर होना चाहिए।

questions.question: An advanced learner once says "He go to school" but uses "goes" correctly elsewhere and self-corrects when asked. According to Corder, this is
questions.questionHi: एक उन्नत विद्यार्थी एक बार "He go to school" कहता है, पर अन्यत्र "goes" सही प्रयोग करता है और पूछने पर स्वयं सुधार लेता है। कॉर्डर के अनुसार यह है
questions.explanation: Corder distinguishes mistakes (random performance slips, self-correctable) from errors (systematic gaps in competence, not self-correctable).
questions.explanationHi: कॉर्डर के अनुसार mistake आकस्मिक निष्पादन-चूक है जिसे स्वयं सुधारा जा सकता है, जबकि error क्षमता की व्यवस्थित कमी है जिसे स्वयं नहीं सुधारा जा सकता।
